title: Would you be little forgiving to not perfect games?
author: adolphite
selftext:
Since trying my hands on making games with AI (not that I have been successful), I have come to realize that game design and eventual shipping is so hard.

Even with AI, I can't seem to get some things right. It got me thinking about how people have made huge open world or complex games without AI in the past.

Are you now willing to give people some slack given the difficulty of making games or you expect them now not to make mistakes given that there's now AI to catch lots of bugs or coding errors?

comments.author: frigginwizard420
comments.body:
dont worry about it  

Make something you like, if other people like it, great  

If you're just into it for the $$, dont bother

comments.author: cowman3456
comments.body:
Mistakes = rushing out a cheap product. 

That's exactly what everybody hates.  If you want to build non-slop, put in the effort.

replies.author: maxneuds
replies.body:
That's it.
With a good idea and proper planning and definitions it's possible to get a good game even from one prompt and some hours of work, but unlikely. Depends a lot also on what assets are needed.

I spend most of my time actually working on assets. That's tough. And for anything with an actual world I find myself that neither 2D nor 3D world by AI is good, that's needs to be hand crafted.

comments.author: Putrid_Clue_2127
comments.body:
My standards for games now aren't really any different than they used to be. If it's fun and doesn't have weird things that break immersion, that's a pretty great start. 

This may sound dumb, but have you tried explaining to the ai you're using what your problem is, and then asking you to help come up with a gameplan for how it could potentially be fixed. Sometimes this gets it thinking about the problem differently itself. 

As someone else has already said, make a game that you'd want to play. Make it FOR you. Then if you like it and get actual gameplay from it, iron out the kinks until it's done and then see if anyone else likes it too. Don't ship it out just to ship it.

I'm currently working on a game I've wanted for years on mobile. It's for me. If others like it, that's great to! But I'm making it to my own gameplay standard. So it's got hundreds of hours of my own time in development so far, and probably about the same amount of time left to go. I'll just be happy when it feels like it's done for me.

comments.author: Big_Birthday_1846
comments.body: it’s not about perfection it’s just them being soulless asf, but you don’t need ai for that, just look at the mainstream industry

comments.author: dedaistgeil
comments.body: Make a good game, it's always about making a good game. A good game needs lots and lots of iteration, testing and polish. Doesn't matter if you use AI or not. AI does not mean you can sit back, type 1 prompt and have the next Skyrim. Even a simple game needs a lot of work with AI to become a marketable product. AI makes the entry easier but the development itself is still hard and takes time.

comments.author: DuckAndQwack
comments.body:
1) It's hard to say, that any of the games are perfect
2) No. If a game is bad (For me) — I won't play in it. If I feel the game good enough — I will play in it

comments.author: Agile_Branch_8743
comments.body:
AI is a tool that supports your existing skills. If you don't know a lot about game design, art direction, coding, etc., AI can't get things right for you.

Most big open world games are built by big teams that combine many different skillsets, usually dedicated to a very specific thing in the game (like artists focusing on trees or stones; not a joke, by the way), with people specialized in helping put all of that together. Then a bunch of people specialized in coming up with the game's concept before any development is done. People dedicated to selling the game.

AI can help you learn from those games, and if you know how to guide it, it can help tackle big chunks of the work. If you don't know what you're doing, I strongly believe AI can make things more difficult for you. Good luck fixing and making all those "omg guys I built this complete game in 3 days" builds fun; it's probably easier to start from scratch.

>Are you now willing to give people some slack given the difficulty of making games

I've always given creators slack. I give less slack to: a) AAA companies releasing incomplete games at full price; b) shovelware, including many of those AI one-shot guys I mentioned.

comments.author: _HoundOfJustice
comments.body: It depends on what exactly we talk about. There are no perfect games. However im very critical of games that are soulless and eventually fully driven by AI with little to none creative footprint and basically typical AI slop. Also people getting overconfident with AI and thinking they gotta build a large scoped game only to make it look empty, bugged as hell, boring are a problem too and their games deserve to be dunked on.

comments.author: Albius
comments.body: Honestly – no. With bigger supply then ever there’s never enough time for all the games. So quality becomes even more of a filter then ever
